```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.width = 7.2, fig.height = 4.6, dpi = 144, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%")
source("figure-style.R")
library(idiographic)
data(srl)
analysis_data <- subset(srl, name %in% c("Aisha", "Alice", "Anika", "Astrid", "Bjorn", "Bob", "Charlie", "Diana", "Erik", "Eve", "Fatima", "Frank"))
```

Person-specific coefficients combine genuine heterogeneity with sampling
error. A learner whose true efficacy slope is 0.30 might produce an estimate
of 0.45 because of noise in a short series. Two functions address this
mixture. `pool_coefs()` estimates the uncertainty-weighted average and the
between-person spread of the true coefficients. `shrink_coefs()` moves each
person's imprecise estimate toward the pooled distribution, producing
stabilised coefficients that separate signal from noise more effectively
than the raw values.

| Question | Function |
|:--|:--|
| What is the uncertainty-weighted average of person-specific coefficients? | `pool_coefs()` |
| How should noisy person-specific coefficients be stabilised? | `shrink_coefs()` |

All examples use 12 learners from the bundled `srl` data, each observed on
154 to 156 days. The individual-scope regression of effort on efficacy and
monitoring serves as the input to both functions.

```{r individual-fit}
individual_fit <- fit_lm(analysis_data, y = "effort",
                         x = c("efficacy", "monitoring"),
                         id = "name", time = "day",
                         scope = "individual")
coefs(individual_fit, scope = "individual", n = 8)
```

Each learner contributes a separate slope and standard error. The standard
errors reflect how precisely each slope is estimated from that learner's
series. Both pooling and shrinkage weight each learner's contribution by
these standard errors, so they require coefficient tables that carry them
--- linear models, generalised linear models, and within--between models
qualify; machine-learning models generally do not.

## `pool_coefs()`

### Analytic question

A DerSimonian--Laird random-effects model treats each person-specific
coefficient as an estimate of that person's true value, observed with
sampling error. The model estimates the
uncertainty-weighted pooled coefficient, the standard deviation of the true
coefficients across persons ($\tau$), and the proportion of observed spread
attributable to genuine between-person differences ($I^2$). Each learner's
coefficient contributes according to its sampling variance, so
well-measured learners receive more weight.

### Pooled estimates

```{r pooling-table}
pooled_coefs <- pool_coefs(individual_fit)
pooled_coefs
```

The pooled efficacy coefficient was 0.29 (95% CI: 0.14 to 0.44). The
estimated $\tau$ was 0.20, and $I^2$ was 0.81 --- roughly four-fifths of the
observed spread among the 12 efficacy slopes reflected true between-person
differences rather than sampling error. Under a normal approximation, the
true slopes of 95% of learners lie between approximately $-$0.10 and 0.68.

The pooled monitoring coefficient was 0.12 (95% CI: $-$0.10 to 0.35), with
$\tau$ = 0.33 and $I^2$ = 0.94. Although the pooled value was compatible
with zero, the large $I^2$ indicates substantial heterogeneity: the
monitoring slope varies considerably across learners, and the pooled mean
does not represent a common effect.

### Visualisation

```{r pooling-plot, fig.cap="Figure 1. Random-effects pooled slopes with 95% confidence intervals. The intercept is omitted because its much larger scale would compress the predictor effects."}
shown_pool <- subset(pooled_coefs, term != "(Intercept)")
forest_plot(shown_pool$estimate, shown_pool$conf_low, shown_pool$conf_high,
            shown_pool$term, xlab = "Random-effects pooled coefficient (95% CI)")
```

The pooled efficacy slope is distinguishable from zero; the monitoring
interval crosses it. These are average values across learners and do not
imply that any individual learner has the pooled slope. The large $I^2$
values confirm that pooled estimates should always be reported together
with $\tau$ and $I^2$.

### Assumptions and failure checks

The DerSimonian--Laird estimator treats learners as independent and assumes
that their true coefficients come from a distribution summarised by a mean
and a variance. The estimator can be imprecise with few learners. $Q$ and
$I^2$ should be read alongside the number of contributing learners and
$\tau$, not in isolation.

At least two learners with finite, positive standard errors are required for
each term. Coefficients with missing or non-positive standard errors are
excluded. Pooling does not turn an associational coefficient into a causal
estimate.

## `shrink_coefs()`

### Analytic question

Empirical-Bayes shrinkage stabilises each person's coefficient by moving it
toward the pooled distribution. The shrinkage weight for each learner is the
ratio of the between-person variance to the sum of the between-person
variance and that learner's sampling variance. A weight near one retains
most of the raw estimate; a weight near zero pulls it toward the pooled
mean. Learners estimated with greater uncertainty are therefore pulled more.

### Shrunken estimates

The same individual fit from the pooling section supplies the raw
coefficients and standard errors.

```{r shrinkage-table}
shrunken_coefs <- shrink_coefs(individual_fit, term = "efficacy")
shrunken_coefs
```

Every efficacy slope was pulled toward the pooled mean of 0.29. The
shrinkage weights ranged from 0.64 (Frank, SE = 0.15) to 0.89 (Eve,
SE = 0.07). Frank's raw slope of 0.12 moved to 0.18; Eve's raw slope of
0.40 moved to 0.39 --- a much smaller shift, because Eve's estimate was
more precise. The three learners with negative raw slopes (Fatima, Astrid,
Diana) were pulled substantially toward the pooled mean, while learners
whose raw slopes were already close to it moved very little.

### Visualisation

```{r shrinkage-plot, fig.cap="Figure 2. Raw (open) and empirical-Bayes shrunken (filled) efficacy coefficients for 12 learners. Longer connecting lines indicate greater shrinkage."}
shrunken_coefs <- shrink_coefs(individual_fit, term = "efficacy",
                               sort_by = "shrunken")
at <- seq_len(nrow(shrunken_coefs))
limits <- range(c(shrunken_coefs$estimate, shrunken_coefs$shrunken, 0))
figure_begin(c(4.2, 7, 1, 1))
plot(shrunken_coefs$shrunken, at, xlim = limits,
     ylim = c(0.5, length(at) + 0.5), yaxt = "n", pch = 21,
     bg = fig_col["teal"], col = "white", cex = 1.3,
     xlab = "Efficacy coefficient", ylab = "")
figure_grid(x = TRUE, y = FALSE)
abline(v = 0, col = fig_col["muted"], lty = 2)
segments(shrunken_coefs$estimate, at, shrunken_coefs$shrunken, at,
         col = fig_col["grid"], lwd = 2.4)
points(shrunken_coefs$estimate, at, pch = 21, bg = "white",
       col = fig_col["muted"], cex = 1.05)
points(shrunken_coefs$shrunken, at, pch = 21, bg = fig_col["teal"],
       col = "white", cex = 1.3)
axis(2, at = at, labels = shrunken_coefs$subject, tick = FALSE,
     col.axis = fig_col["ink"])
legend("bottomright", c("Raw", "Shrunken"), pch = 21,
       pt.bg = c("white", fig_col["teal"]),
       col = c(fig_col["muted"], "white"), bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
```

Extreme raw values were drawn toward the pooled centre, and precise
estimates moved less. The shrinkage pattern is visible in the connecting
lines: Fatima, Astrid, and Diana (the leftmost points) have the longest
lines, whereas Eve and Bjorn (near the pooled mean with small standard
errors) barely moved. The weight column in the printed output quantifies
how much of each learner's own estimate was retained.

### Assumptions and failure checks

Empirical-Bayes shrinkage inherits the random-effects assumptions from
`pool_coefs()`: independent learners and a coefficient distribution
summarised by one mean and variance. A multimodal coefficient distribution
--- two groups with genuinely different slopes --- makes one pooled centre
inadequate. In such cases, subgroup-specific shrinkage would be more
appropriate; `test_subgroups()` can assess whether a multi-group
representation is supported.

Standard errors are required; coefficients without them are excluded. The
shrunken estimates are appropriate for description and stabilised
prediction. Their usual intervals require additional modelling if formal
person-specific inference is the goal.

## Choice between the two functions

`pool_coefs()` addresses the population: what is the average person-specific
slope, how much do the true slopes vary, and how much of the observed spread
reflects sampling error? `shrink_coefs()` addresses each person: what is a
more stable estimate of this person's slope after accounting for
imprecision?

Raw individual coefficients remain appropriate when each person has enough
observations to produce estimates with small standard errors. When standard
errors are large relative to the between-person spread, shrinkage moves the
noisiest estimates toward the pooled mean and the improvement is greatest.

Neither function asserts that every person has the pooled effect.
`fit_lm(scope = "pooled")` estimates one row-level regression --- a
different question from meta-analytic pooling of individual slopes.
`test_subgroups()` should be consulted before replacing a continuous
coefficient distribution with discrete classes.
